Issued at 214 PM CDT Sun Jul 26 2026

Tonight and Monday Morning...

The forecast through Monday remains complex and highly
uncertain, although some of the main key players are coming a 
bit better into focus. Still, the forecast evolution tonight 
will hinge on several low-predictability aspects, including 
whether storms congeal into a forward-propagating complex and do
so early enough in the MCS lifecyle to direct a southward- 
moving cold pool into our region (as opposed to shifting off to 
the east). 

The main feature of interest is a 700-500 mb shortwave currently 
straddling the International Border in southern Manitoba.
Elevated convection has been ongoing since earlier this morning
with this feature. Guidance has been all over the place 
regarding convective evolution, and presumably some of the 
variability has to do with the magnitude of inhibition from the 
Minnesota Arrowhead, eastward into northern Wisconsin and the 
western Upper Peninsula. It's unclear if wildfire smoke might be
playing a role in slightly stunting insolation a bit, but given
the limited extent and vertical depth of any Cu corroborates the
significant analyzed MLCIN at this hour. Earlier runs of the 
HRRR, which aggressively convected in this area mid-late 
afternoon have notably backed off on this outcome, likely due to
increased inhibition. 

If this initial activity does not materialize upstream, there's
been a secondary signal for storm development across 
central/eastern Iowa early this evening within the heart of the 
MUCAPE axis. Should this materialize, steering flow and the 
instability gradient orientation should generally keep activity 
to our west and south although this may impinge on our far 
southwest locales late in the evening. 

There's perhaps a better chance for storms to develop later 
this evening well to the north as the main body of the 
aforementioned shortwave and attendant forcing shifts across the
Arrowhead, eventually congealing into a forward-propagating 
MCS. Exactly when and how far east this takes place will play a 
critical role in our storm chances overnight and into Monday 
morning, as a more disorganized complex would shift far enough 
east to largely miss our area, while a more quickly-organizing 
complex would tend to dive southward along the eastern fringes 
of the main MUCAPE gradient and along the 850-300 mb thickness 
contours. Given the progged orientation of the instability 
gradient and upper jet nosing off just to our east, suspect the 
chances for thunderstorm activity will maximize during the late
overnight and early Monday morning timeframe. Any MCS would 
encounter increasing nocturnal CIN, but sufficient deep layer 
shear would support sustenance to some degree into our area, 
mainly with a threat for localized damaging wind gusts. 

Monday afternoon and evening...

Assuming convection departs the region through midday, some
airmass recovery would be likely during the afternoon as anvil 
debris is carried away from the region and breezy southwesterly 
boundary layer flow develops. With sufficient insolation, 
temperatures could crawl back towards 90, and dewpoints would 
likely surge back into the mid to upper 70s. This would set the 
stage for another round of potentially severe convection very 
late in the afternoon and into Monday evening as an elongated 
surface low drags a cold front into and eventually through the 
region. 

While a robust shortwave trough will precede the front, it
remains unclear if thunderstorms will manage to re-develop 
during this period as a plume of incredibly dry mid-level air 
(700 mb dewpoints progged near -30 C) will rapidly surge 
eastward during the early evening. This stronger forcing may lag
just enough to preclude CI prior to the loss of daytime heating
and quickly-increasing MLCIN. However, if a storm or two 
manages to fire, the kinematic environment is concerning, 
particularly across northeast Illinois and northwest Indiana 
where deep layer shear will be maximized (near 50 knots) along 
with notable clockwise low-level hodograph curvature. In this 
scenario, convective coverage might not be particularly high, 
but the ceiling on an individual cell or two would be 
significant, including the threat for tornadoes. Finally, there 
would be a potential for a supercell to anchor on the incoming 
boundary or composite outflow/lake breeze which could pose a 
localized flash flood threat. All of this remains low confidence
though, and will depend to a large degree on how overnight and 
morning convective episodes play out.

undisturbed environment, peak heat indices would easily push
